row.note: When Moses' hands grow heavy, Aaron and Hur seat him and hold them up, one on each side, until sunset; the commentary's exhausted walker is likewise sustained between companions, making dependence a shared act.
An angel returns, touches Elijah, and tells him to rise and eat because the journey is too much for him; this verse recognizes dependence before onward travel, matching the commentary's need for aid.
After eating, Elijah rises and travels forty days in the strength of that food; this gives a concrete result for the aid sought by the commentary's weakened traveler: renewed ability to walk onward.

Moses recalls that YHWH carried Israel through the wilderness as a man carries his son; the traveling people depend on support through the whole route, extending the commentary's individual image to a community.

row.basis: ק־ו־ם, raising the one who stumbles
row.note: The source commentary labels Arabic ق و م (q-w-m) for stopping and standing upright; Job's Hebrew יְקִימוּן (yəqîmûn, from קום) says Job's words used to raise a stumbling person and strengthen weak knees, a cognate use that restores rather than halts movement.
The verse says that if one falls, the other can raise his companion; it makes explicit the human help implicit in the commentary's walker leaning on two people.
The speaker is drawn from a pit and mire, set on rock, and given firm steps; the rescue turns being stuck into supported movement, like the commentary's stopped mount and restored walker.
Even when the righteous person falls, he is not cast down because YHWH holds his hand; this directly pictures the support that keeps a weak walker from collapsing.
The speaker says that when his foot was slipping, YHWH's steadfast love supported him; the same bodily danger and sustaining aid appear in the commentary's stumbling traveler.
YHWH supports all who fall and straightens all who are bowed down; the verse joins the commentary's two bodily states, loss of footing and needing to be brought upright.

Wilderness wanderers cry to YHWH in distress and he rescues them; the surrounding scene is people lost, hungry, and thirsty, so this is a specific travel crisis answered by the aid the commentary says a traveler needs.
YHWH leads the rescued group by a straight way to an inhabited city; it unites the commentary's request for help with its request to be guided along a straight path.
The shepherd leads the speaker in paths of righteousness; this is a prayerful image of being guided along a good way, adding the relation of trust between guide and dependent traveler.
As the speaker walks through a dark valley, the shepherd's rod and staff comfort him; a tangible support accompanies the walk, complementing the commentary's image of a body steadied by others.
The pilgrim answers that his help comes from YHWH, maker of heaven and earth; this gives a concrete divine answer to the commentary's question of what a dependent traveler can rely on.
YHWH leads returning Israelites to streams of water by a straight road on which they will not stumble; the promised route closely joins guidance, sustenance, and secure walking as in the commentary.
The prophet tells the community to strengthen slack hands and make firm weak knees; this names the bodily weakness that the commentary gives to its traveler before he can walk uprightly.
The community is told to speak courage to fearful hearts because God comes to save; alongside the commentary's physical supports, this shows encouragement as aid to the weak.
The lame leap like a deer when the wilderness blossoms; this turns the commentary's halted, exhausted movement into restored mobility.

row.basis: God leads on an unknown road
row.note: YHWH promises to lead the blind by roads they have not known, make rough places level, and not forsake them; the passage joins guidance with hands-on provision for a dependent traveler.
The speaker says he has taught the way of wisdom and led his pupil in upright tracks; this gives a concrete teacher-and-traveler counterpart to asking for guidance on a straight way.
The pupil's stride will not be hampered and he will not stumble when running; this describes the bodily result of the guidance and steadiness developed in the commentary.

row.basis: Arms that teach a child to walk
row.note: YHWH says he taught Ephraim to walk and took them in his arms, though they did not recognize that he healed them; the image presents guidance and support as care a dependent person may not even perceive.

The person who trusts YHWH is like a tree planted by water whose roots reach the stream and whose leaf stays green in drought; this gives a living image for the commentary's tree standing on its roots, with hidden nourishment preserving stability.

The source commentary labels Arabic ع ب د for نَعْبُدُ; Hebrew תַּעַבְדוּן (ta'avdun, root עבד) is its cognate in God's promise that liberated Israel will serve him at the mountain, adding the setting of worship as service after deliverance.

The source commentary labels Arabic م ل ك for مَٰلِكِ; Hebrew מֶלֶךְ (melekh, root מלך) appears as YHWH is named Israel's judge, lawgiver, and king who saves, joining royal authority with the rescue sought by the dependent.

The nations are told that YHWH reigns, establishes the world, and judges peoples equitably; this directly connects the selected ayah's sovereign over the Day of Judgment with the commentary's root image of firm, sustaining authority.
YHWH comes to judge the earth in righteousness and faithfulness; this supplies a specific Hebrew Bible scene of the judgment day named in the selected ayah.
In the passage's eschatological day, YHWH becomes king over all the earth; it closely joins the selected ayah's kingship and judgment-day language.
The Ancient of Days takes his seat, the court sits, and books are opened; this is an apocalyptic judgment scene to place beside the selected ayah's day of reckoning.
In Zechariah's blessing, God will guide the feet of those in darkness into the way of peace; its prayer-like language explicitly joins guidance, feet, and a path as the commentary does.

The Samaritan binds the wounded man's injuries, puts him on his own animal, and brings him to an inn; the story reverses the commentary's exhausted mount but shares its precise scene of a vulnerable traveler kept moving by another's practical care.

The Samaritan pays the innkeeper and promises further expenses for the wounded traveler; this extends the commentary's image of leaning on support into sustained care beyond the first act of getting someone upright.

row.basis: No one to help him reach the water
row.note: The disabled man says he has no one to put him in the pool and another enters first; his particular inability to move without assistance embodies the commentary's dependent traveler asking for support.
Jesus tells the man to rise, take his mat, and walk; the command's result is a body restored to upright movement, the outcome pictured in the commentary's supported traveler.

row.basis: A hand raises the lame man
row.note: Peter takes the lame man by the right hand and raises him; his feet and ankles become strong and he walks, making the commentary's transition from aid to upright walking an enacted healing scene.

Jesus lays hands on a woman bent for eighteen years and she immediately stands straight and glorifies God; the scene joins bodily restoration to praise, as the commentary joins uprightness with worship.
The author urges readers to lift drooping hands and strengthen weakened knees; this directly names the bodily frailty behind the commentary's request for help.
The author tells the community to make straight paths for their feet so the lame may be healed; it closely joins the commentary's weak walker, straight way, and restored gait.

Readers are invited to approach the throne of grace for mercy and timely help; the passage gives a prayerful counterpart to worship joined with asking for aid, and recasts approach to divine authority as confidence in receiving support.
Paul says God fixed a day to judge the world in righteousness through an appointed man; this directly elaborates the judgment-day claim in the selected ayah.
The Son of Man comes in glory with angels and sits on his throne; the scene gives the selected ayah's sovereign on Judgment Day a concrete Christian apocalyptic counterpart.
The dead stand before the great throne as books are opened and they are judged by what is written; this supplies a distinct vision of the day of reckoning named in the selected ayah.

The Babylonian Talmud's Tefillat ha-Derekh asks God to lead the traveler in peace, direct his steps, and support him; it is a Jewish liturgical form joining the commentary's requests for help and a straight path.

The Talmud asks whether Moses' raised hands themselves won the battle, then explains Israel's victory through looking upward and directing their hearts to God; it turns bodily support into a lesson about the prayerful dependence beside the commentary's image.

row.basis: A hand lifts the suffering person
row.note: Rabbi Yohanan visits the ill Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba, takes his hand, and raises him; the passage says a captive cannot free himself, making dependence on another's help explicit.
Among the morning blessings is praise of God as the one who straightens the bent; this Jewish liturgical wording joins bodily uprightness to praise, matching a secondary image in the commentary.

The Lord's Prayer asks not to be brought into trial and asks for deliverance from evil; this is a specific communal petition for divine help alongside the commentary's prayer that worshippers cannot proceed alone.
Paul tells the community to help the weak and be patient with everyone; this makes the commentary's two-sided human support an ethical duty within a worshipping community.

The psalm says a person's steps are established by YHWH and that he delights in the person's way; it adds divine ordering of the walk to the commentary's request for guidance, though this verse does not itself describe a stumble.

At the crossroads, the people are told to ask for the ancient paths, find the good way, and walk in it for rest; this makes seeking guidance an explicit act, though Jeremiah's audience refuses the invitation.

Those who wait for YHWH renew strength and walk without fainting; the verse supplies endurance for the commentary's weakened traveler, while its running image differs from the commentary's calm, non-fugitive gait.

After the court scene, one like a son of man receives everlasting dominion and all peoples serve him; this places universal service beside the commentary's sovereign and worship, while Daniel distinguishes the enthroned judge from the figure given dominion.

row.basis: A difficult way leading to life
row.note: Jesus describes the narrow gate and hard way that lead to life, with few finding them; this makes the requested path a morally consequential course, while the surah's surrounding verse specifies its own blessed and rejected ways.
Paul says the strong ought to bear the weaknesses of those without strength rather than please themselves; this turns the commentary's supported walk into a concrete communal obligation.
Paul commands believers to carry one another's burdens; this gives the commentary's image of leaning on another person an ethical, shared form.

The Community Rule describes two spirits and the opposed ways they lead people to walk; this Jewish interpretive framework makes a request for the straight path a choice of moral allegiance, rather than only a route.
The Didache opens by naming a way of life and a way of death; it gives the commentary's requested way a concrete ethical alternative in early Christian teaching.
While reflecting on chastity, Augustine asks God to grant what God commands; this makes the commentary's pairing of worship and help a claim about moral action itself needing divine support.

Augustine reads the wounded traveler as fallen humanity and the Samaritan as Christ; this Christian interpretation shifts Luke's practical aid scene toward divine rescue, a useful contrast with the commentary's human shoulders and support.

In the Song at the Sea, YHWH leads the people he redeemed and guides them by his strength to his holy dwelling; it joins rescue, help, and a destination on the journey the commentary asks God to guide.

Moses recalls YHWH leading Israel through a great, dangerous wilderness and bringing water from flint; the community's physical dependence on guidance and sustenance closely expands the commentary's tired traveler.

row.basis: The guide goes before and does not abandon
row.note: Moses tells Joshua that YHWH goes before him and will not fail or forsake him; it makes the sought guidance personal and reassuring for someone unable to proceed alone.

In a communal confession, the people say God sustained them in the wilderness for forty years, their clothes did not wear out and their feet did not swell; it makes divine aid concrete in the body of travelers.
YHWH makes the speaker's feet like a deer's and sets him on secure heights; it pictures strength and stable footing after the commentary's image of a halted, unsteady traveler.

row.basis: A broad place for each step
row.note: The speaker says God enlarged the place beneath his steps so his feet did not slip; this gives a direct image of supported walking and secure footing.
The speaker says his foot stands on level ground and blesses YHWH in the assembly; it joins stable posture with worship, two elements the commentary brings together in the needy traveler's prayer.
The psalm says God keeps the community alive and does not let its feet slip; this is a specific image of ongoing support for people who could otherwise fall.

row.basis: A flock led by two human guides
row.note: The psalm says God led his people like a flock by the hand of Moses and Aaron; divine guidance is mediated through two human leaders, adding a communal counterpart to the commentary's walker leaning between two people.
The speaker says YHWH rescued his soul from death, his eyes from tears, and his feet from stumbling; the last detail explicitly links divine rescue to continued walking.

row.basis: A level path for the righteous
row.note: The prophet says the path of the righteous is level and God makes it smooth; this sharpens the commentary's image of guidance into a road made passable for the walker.

row.basis: Direction when turning right or left
row.note: The people hear a voice behind them saying, “This is the way; walk in it,” when they turn right or left; it uniquely connects guidance with the commentary's side-to-side swaying walker.

row.basis: A safe highway for the redeemed
row.note: Isaiah continues the restoration scene with a highway called the holy way, on which even the travelers will not stray; it supplies the safe, morally directed road that follows the weak hands and knees in the same chapter.

row.basis: The shepherd carries and gently leads
row.note: YHWH gathers lambs in his arm, carries them close, and gently leads those with young; the verse gives a concrete image of help adjusted to a traveler's weakness.
YHWH tells fearful Israel not to fear, promises help, and says he will uphold them with his righteous hand; the bodily act of holding someone up closely matches the commentary's dependent walker.

row.basis: A word that sustains the weary
row.note: The servant says God gives him a trained tongue to sustain the weary with a word; this adds speech as support alongside the commentary's shoulders, upright body, and calm gait.
The proverb says to acknowledge YHWH in all one's ways and he will make the paths straight; this is a direct formulation of asking God to guide one along a straight way.
The pupil will walk securely and his foot will not stumble; this states the bodily result of the steady path and support developed in the commentary.
YHWH is the pupil's confidence and keeps his foot from being caught; the verse makes divine reliance a protection for the body's movement.

row.basis: Make the path level for your feet
row.note: The wisdom teacher tells the pupil to make a level path for his feet and make all his ways sure; this continues the same chapter's taught walk with an explicit act of stabilizing the road.
The pupil is told not to swerve right or left but to turn his foot away from evil; this adds a moral direction to the commentary's image of swaying from side to side.

row.basis: A lifted yoke and food for the dependent
row.note: YHWH describes leading Ephraim with human kindness, lifting the yoke from its jaws, and bending down to feed it; it adds gentle, practical care for a dependent being to the commentary's exhausted mount and traveler.

row.basis: Worship with a textual variant about support
row.note: WLC's ketiv vocalizes the final noun as “bed,” while its qere reads “staff”; only the qere makes Jacob's worship explicitly lean on a support, so this verse should preserve the distinction rather than silently treating the staff as WLC's written reading.

row.basis: Jacob worships leaning on his staff
row.note: Hebrews recounts Jacob blessing Joseph's sons and worshiping while leaning on his staff, following the Greek reading of Genesis 47:31; it makes worship and physical support occur together, exactly the pairing developed in the commentary.

row.basis: A sinking walker cries for help
row.note: Peter begins to sink while walking on the water and cries, “Lord, save me”; this is a precise scene of someone whose movement fails and who asks another for immediate aid.

row.basis: A hand catches the failing walker
row.note: Jesus immediately reaches out and catches Peter; the physical rescue answers the cry for help and supplies the hand support missing from the commentary's faltering traveler.

row.basis: A roadside traveler asks for mercy
row.note: Near Jericho, the blind man Bartimaeus cries to Jesus for mercy as Jesus passes; his vulnerable position on the road and direct plea for help make the need for assistance concrete.

row.basis: Restored sight and a guided way
row.note: The healed man follows Jesus on the way, glorifying God; it joins recovery of a dependent person, continued movement, and worship as the commentary does.

row.basis: Friends carry a man who cannot walk
row.note: Four people bring a paralyzed man to Jesus on a mat; their coordinated carrying makes the commentary's reliance on other bodies literal and communal.

row.basis: The Spirit helps weakness in prayer
row.note: Paul says the Spirit helps believers in their weakness because they do not know how to pray as they ought; this closely links the commentary's inability to proceed alone with its joining worship and a request for help.

row.basis: Kept from stumbling and presented standing
row.note: The doxology praises God as able to keep believers from stumbling and present them blameless before his glory; it turns the commentary's bodily image of being steadied into a promise about standing securely before God.
Jesus continues the throne scene by gathering all nations and separating them; this supplies the judgment action following the royal appearance in the preceding verse of the same passage.

row.basis: Do not rely on your own understanding
row.note: The proverb tells the pupil not to lean on his own understanding but to trust YHWH; this makes dependence explicit beside the commentary's image of a traveler who cannot support himself, though the proverb speaks metaphorically.

row.basis: A reader asks for someone to guide him
row.note: The Ethiopian official says he cannot understand Isaiah unless someone guides him; this shifts the commentary's dependent traveler's need for guidance to interpretation, showing why a guide may be needed even by a capable traveler.

row.basis: A companion joins travelers on the road
row.note: As two disciples walk sadly toward Emmaus, Jesus draws near and walks with them; this echoes the commentary's image of a vulnerable walk made in company, though the aid is companionship rather than physical support.

row.basis: A guide interprets the road's meaning
row.note: Jesus interprets Moses and the prophets to the two travelers; this adds scriptural instruction to the commentary's image of a guide who helps a dependent person find the way.
The author quotes the confession that the Lord is one's helper and therefore one need not fear; it gives a direct first-person expression of reliance, though it does not develop the travel image.

The Didache instructs its hearer to give to everyone who asks; within its teaching on the way of life, it makes the commentary's image of receiving support into a concrete obligation to support others.
